payload.message:
test(desktop): add a Svelte component test harness

Vitest now runs as two projects. `node` keeps the pure logic fast — no Svelte
compiler, no jsdom — and `dom` mounts real components; a module that needs a
`document` to be tested is a module with UI concerns in it, so the split is
also a design signal. Component tests are `*.svelte.test.ts`, which is how the
node project knows to skip them.

The double sits **below** `src/lib/api.ts`, not in place of it. Mocking the API
module would mean the mock becomes the assertion, and it drifts the first time a
command is renamed. Tauri's own `mockIPC` replaces the IPC transport instead, so
`api.ts` runs for real — its command names, its argument marshalling — and only
the process on the other side is fake.

`src/test/tauri.ts` adds what a bare `mockIPC` lacks: a typed handler table
where an unhandled command rejects loudly rather than returning `undefined`
(which would surface later as a confusing null-deref inside the component), a
call log, event emission, and failure/latency injection. `render.ts` pairs a
component with a backend and tears both down together; `setup.dom.ts` fills
jsdom's gaps once and promotes an unknown-prop or lifecycle warning to a failure.

Three config details that each cost a debugging session, all commented in place:
`svelte.config.js` is ignored (its `vitePreprocess` needs a Vite environment a
Vitest worker does not have), `mainFields` prefers `module` (a dependency ships
only an `.mjs` while declaring a `main` that does not exist), and `conditions`
must list `svelte` alongside Vite's defaults.

No production code changed.

test(desktop): cover three components at the behaviour level Chosen for what they can get wrong, not for being easy to render. `UsageMeter` is shared by the provider cards and the status-bar popover, so a change moves two surfaces at once: the number a user reads must match what the backend reported, the bar must stay inside its track, and a nearly-empty bar must still be visible — 0 % rendering as nothing looks like a broken widget. `SaveDiscardDialog` answers "save, discard, or stay?" through a promise the tab-close path is awaiting. Every route out of it must resolve that promise, Escape included: a route that resolves nothing leaves the caller awaiting forever and the tab simply never closes, with no error anywhere. `AgentLogo` exercises the whole seam — it renders, asks the real API layer for a logo, and re-renders on the answer. Its fallback chain is also the kind of logic that looks obviously correct and silently was not: every favicon-backed logo rendered as the generic glyph for a long time because the URL went straight into an `` the CSP refused.

test(desktop): add backend integration tests against a real filesystem

`src-tauri/tests/` did not exist. The automations store is a good first tenant:
the headless runner and the app each open their own over the same directory, so
the round trip across a process boundary is a real contract rather than an
implementation detail.

Ten tests over a `TempDir`, using only the crate's public surface — which is what
keeps them integration tests instead of unit tests with a longer path. They cover
the round trip, replace-not-append, seed-once (including after the user deletes
the examples), a truncated file degrading rather than panicking, nothing written
outside the store's own root, and a path with spaces and non-ASCII characters.

The automation is written out in full rather than via `Default`, so adding a
required field to the model breaks this file — which is the point of a test over
a persisted shape.

test(desktop): add fixtures a test cannot escape

The fake `gh` refuses to run without an explicit latch, scrubs anything
credential-shaped out of its log, and fails loudly on a command nobody stubbed
— silence there would mean the caller parses an empty string and asserts
something meaningless.

The PATH shim is the part that matters. It builds a directory holding only
fakes, so every CLI the app shells out to resolves inside it and a test that
forgets to stub one gets "blocked by the test harness" instead of talking to
real GitHub. `assertNoRealCli` re-checks that claim rather than trusting it. Two
things that look right and are not: resolving a name by spawning `where` cannot
work when the shimmed PATH no longer contains System32, and Node has refused to
spawn `.cmd` directly since the BatBadBut hardening — so lookup is done in
process and the shim tests go through a shell.

Also disposable and legacy app profiles for the migration paths, and a port test
covering the case the app avoids by never naming a port: asking for 0 survives a
crowded machine, asking for a taken one does not. The second half is what gives
the first half meaning.

The git repository, the stand-in agent and the loopback server are shared with
the resource benchmarks rather than copied — two generators would drift, and the
repo fixture is only useful because its commit hash is pinned.

test(desktop): make the coverage matrix a checked file, not a claim

A coverage table in prose is worth what checks it, which is nothing: every row
gets ticked and none gets verified. This one is data, and a test reads it back
against the repository — a flow claiming a layer must cite a file that exists
(globs must match something), a partially covered flow must state its gap, and
no flow may list a layer as both covered and planned.

It records what is *not* tested as carefully as what is, because that is the
half a reader cannot otherwise discover.

test(desktop): drive the real app end to end

Eight journeys over a release binary, its Rust backend, a real WebView2 and real
IPC: launch, session restore, terminals in a split, a sleeping workspace, a git
project, an agent and the hook chain, the browser window, and a profile written
by an older build.

Each spec is one journey with its own app, started from a profile seeded for it.
Setting a journey up by clicking is how an E2E suite becomes slow and brittle —
twenty clicks to reach the thing you wanted to assert, any of which can break for
an unrelated reason — so setup is seeded and the assertions still go through the
real UI, real IPC and a real backend.

Four things about this layer that are not guessable, all commented where they
bite:

- `tauri-driver` hands you a webview at `about:blank`. It does not attach to the
  window the app already navigated, so every query succeeds and returns an empty
  document — which reads as "the app rendered nothing" while the app is running
  perfectly. The session navigates to the app's own origin, and IPC is live
  there: `invoke("ping")` answers from Rust.
- `tauri:options.env` never reached the app. A diagnostic run came up on the
  developer's real profile, showing their actual projects; a journey that removed
  a worktree would have removed a real one. The variable is set on the driver,
  and `before` refuses to run unless the app shows exactly what was seeded.
- WebdriverIO evaluates the config twice, once per process. A `mkdtemp` profile
  therefore exists twice: the driver points at one, the seed writes the other,
  and the app comes up empty whatever a journey asked for. The path is fixed.
- The app is found by executable name, which is safe only because the pre-flight
  refuses to start beside another instance. Matching the profile directory —
  the apparently safer choice — matches nothing, since `UXNAN_DATA_DIR` is an
  environment variable; what it did match was the PowerShell process running the
  query, so the reaper spent several runs killing its own query and reporting
  success.

Assertions ask the backend over IPC rather than reading the screen: the UI is
localised, so an assertion on visible text is an assertion on a translation. A
terminal's contents are unreadable either way — xterm paints through WebGL — so
"is a shell alive" is answered from the process tree.

Teardown reaps by pid and waits for the processes to actually go. The agent
journey closes the app on purpose, to prove the agent it started does not outlive
it.

24 tests, ~39 s for the suite, green on consecutive runs with nothing left
behind.

ci(desktop): run component tests in the gate, E2E on its own schedule

Component tests join the required job immediately: they are fast, and they catch
the mounting and wiring failures unit tests structurally cannot.

E2E gets its own on-demand/nightly Windows workflow. It needs a release build, a
WebDriver matched to the runner's WebView2 and a machine with no other uxnan
running, and it is deliberately **not** blocking yet — requiring it before it has
a track record on that runner is how a gate earns a reputation for false failures
and gets switched off. It uploads a screenshot and the page source per failed
test.

The build step is `tauri build --no-bundle`, not `cargo build --release`: without
the `custom-protocol` feature the binary stays in dev mode and loads
`localhost:1420`, so the app would run with no UI and every assertion would fail
for the wrong reason.

docs(desktop): document the test pyramid and the manual layer

`docs/testing.md` gains the layer model (what each of L0–L5 proves, and which
one a given change needs), the component-test conventions, the driver decision
with the comparison that produced it, a flake policy — quarantine with an owner
and a 14-day limit, keep the case at a lower layer, one retry for infrastructure
only, fix the wait rather than the timeout — and an **L5 checklist**: the twelve
things no automated layer can honestly cover, each with why it cannot be
automated here and a column for when it was last verified.

The spec side, per the drift rule: `04-technical-reference.md` records the
pyramid under Phase 5 as a post-plan addition, including what the implementation
did differently from the sketch it replaced.

Counts re-derived rather than incremented on trust: 565 Vitest across two
projects, 387 Rust (377 unit + 10 integration), 24 E2E tests across 8 journeys.

payload.message:
fix(desktop): resolve the fake gh path the same way on every platform

The fixture test located `fake-gh.mjs` with `new URL(import.meta.url).pathname`
and stripped the leading slash. That slash is a drive-letter artefact on Windows
and *part of the path* everywhere else, so the test passed here and handed Node a
relative `home/runner/…` on the Linux and macOS runners — which it then resolved
against the working directory, producing a doubled path and seven failures with
nothing wrong underneath them.

`fileURLToPath` is the API for this and has no platform branch.
